texts.label: text
texts.orig: Surprisingly, Steve Jobs and Mike Tyson have the same career advice: You can plan all you want, but it won’t work out the way you expect. Instead, they suggest, follow your interests — be they building computers or punching people in the mouth — and only looking backward will it make any sense.

texts.orig: When I was in high school, the main thing I knew was that I wanted to work with computers. I read every computer programming book I could find (often buying, reading, and returning them to save money 🤫). This led me to a number of odd jobs fixing, teaching, and programming computers. Which led me to study computer science in college. Which led me to a job as an engineer at a startup, which led me to start my own company, which led me to join Airbnb, which unexpectedly led me to this newsletter adventure.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I was at my first job out of college for nine years. I was at my second job (not counting my startup) for seven years. Loyalty is great, and you learn a lot sticking with a problem and an organization for a long period of time, but looking back, I got a bit too comfy and stuck around too long. And when I think about the most pivotal moments in my career, they always came at the end of these long stretches: Leaving that first job led to my startup, and leaving that second job led to this newsletter.

texts.orig: For sure get to know your future hiring manager and your future team before you take a role, but also focus on the company culture. People will come and go, but the culture will remain. Ask yourself: Does this company attract the kind of people I want to work with? Will they push me to get better? And are these the people who I aspire to become?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I took the test in a small room inside an adult computer training school in Los Angeles. As I was leaving to go home, after completing (and passing) the test, I walked past a lady who happened to run the school. She looked at me — a 16-year-old kid taking this test that normally only middle-aged IT professionals take, and on the spot offered me a job to teach at the school.
